simple: Scope means where in your script a variable can be seen and used. A `local` variable only exists inside the block of code where you made it, like inside a function or loop. Inner blocks can see variables from outer blocks, but outer blocks cannot peek inside inner ones. Understanding scope stops a lot of confusing bugs, like a variable suddenly being `nil`.
analogy: Scope is like rooms in a house with one-way windows. From a small inner room you can look out and see everything in the bigger rooms around you, but people in the big rooms cannot see into the small room.
keyPoints: A block is the body of a function, loop, or `if` statement.
Local variables can be used in the block where they are made and in any blocks inside it, but not outside.
Global variables (no `local`) can be used anywhere in the same script, but not from other scripts.
Prefer `local`: it is faster (globals can make a busy loop more than 10% slower) and is cleaned up when its block ends.
To share values between scripts, use a ModuleScript.
Capturing: a function can use a local variable from the block around it. That captured variable is called an upvalue.
Shadowing: making a new `local` with the same name inside an inner block. The outer one is not changed.
`const` variables follow the same scope rules as `local` ones.

terms.scope: The area of code where a variable or function can be used.
terms.block: A chunk of code inside a function, loop, or `if`, usually ending with `end`.
terms.parent block / child block: A child block sits inside a parent block. A loop inside a function is the function's child block.
terms.local scope: Only usable in the block where it was made (and blocks inside it).
terms.global scope: Usable anywhere in the same script.
terms.hash lookup: A slower way Luau finds global variables, by searching for the name each time.
terms.capture: When a function uses a local variable from outside itself.
terms.upvalue: A local variable from an outer block that a function uses (captures).
terms.shadowing: Making a new local with the same name in an inner block. Inside, the new one hides the outer one; outside, the outer one is unchanged.
terms.ModuleScript: A special script that returns values or functions other scripts can load with `require`.

example.title: See scope and shadowing in action
example.code:
local score = 10 -- local to the whole script

local function addBonus()
	-- This function can see score from the outer block (capture)
	score += 5
	local bonusText = "Bonus added!" -- only exists inside this function
	print(bonusText)
end

addBonus()
print(score) --> 15
print(bonusText) --> nil (it was local to addBonus)

for i = 1, 2 do
	local score = 100 -- a new shadow variable, only inside the loop
	print("Loop score:", score) --> 100
end

print("Real score:", score) --> 15 (unchanged by the loop)
explain: `score` is made at the top, so everything below can use it.
`addBonus` captures `score` and changes it from 10 to 15.
`bonusText` lives only inside `addBonus`, so printing it outside gives `nil`.
Inside the loop, `local score = 100` makes a separate variable that hides the outer one.
After the loop, the original `score` is still 15.

watchOut: Using a variable outside the block it was made in. It will be `nil`; declare it in an outer block instead.
Accidentally shadowing. Writing `local score = ...` inside a function makes a new variable instead of changing the outer one.
Forgetting `local` inside a function. That makes a global by mistake.
Expecting another script to see your variables. Use a ModuleScript to share them.
